text.p: British supermarket group J. Sainsbury Plc said on Tuesday that it had appointed a second broker to strengthen its team of advisers.

The company, which is trying to regain sales momentum after being toppled from the top slot by rival Tesco over a year ago, said in a statement it had appointed Hoare Govett Corporate Finance Limited to act jointly with existing brokers SBC Warburg.
Sainsbury said the move was "to provide additional access to corporate finance and equity research capabilities."

"We have chosen to strengthen our team of advisers...Hoare Govett...will work alongside SBC Warburg to provide us with a team of outstanding expertise and service," finance director Rosemary Thorne said in a statement.
"It would give them a degree of flexibility for the future," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.

But some analysts said the move could also reflect the group's attempts to improve investor relations, which fell to a low point at the beginning of the year when it issued a surprise profits warning.
It shocked the market in January when it warned that profits would fall some 150 million pounds ($246.6 million) short of expectations as it tried to push sales.
"In investor relations terms, Sainsbury have done a poor job over the last year or so," said one analyst who asked not to be identified.
"The profits warning at the start of this year left quite a few people none too happy," he added.
Shares, which had underperformed the sector since October 1996, slumped nearly 50 pence to 341 pence after the profits warning.
Prices continued to slide through to the beginning of March, when they reached a low for the year of around 307 pence, but have since made some recovery.
They were bolstered by year profits of 651 million pounds at the beginning of May, a fraction above the company's January forecast but still 14 percent down from a year ago.
Shares were standing at 363 pence by 1107 GMT on Tuesday, down four pence on the day.
Sainsbury now claims to have turned the tide of sliding turnover with current sales from existing stores up 4.2 percent from four percent gains in the 16 weeks to January 11.
The company maintained the decision to move to a joint brokerage followed a trend among around 70 percent of London's top 100 quoted stocks.
"It gives us more expertise, more experience," a spokesman said.
